behavioral.why: They check your story is coherent and relevant to this role, in 2 minutes.
tips: Present → past → future: what you do now, what brought you here, why this role next.
Pick 2–3 achievements that match the job description.
Stay under 2 minutes; end on why you are here.
behavioral.model: I'm a data analyst with two years in retail analytics, where I build Power BI reports used by 40 store managers. Before that I studied statistics and did an internship in a logistics company, where I automated a weekly report in Python and saved the team half a day each week. I'm now looking to move closer to data engineering, building the pipelines behind those reports, which is exactly what this role offers.

behavioral.q: Why do you want to join our company?
behavioral.why: They test whether you researched them and will stay.
tips: Mention something specific: product, mission, tech stack, recent news.
Link it to your own goals and skills.
Avoid salary, location or 'it's a big name' as the main reason.
behavioral.model: I use your product myself and I read your engineering blog post about moving to dbt and Snowflake. I want to work on a modern data stack at your scale, and my experience with SQL modelling and data quality checks fits the challenges described in the post.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a time you worked in a team to deliver something difficult.
behavioral.why: Collaboration matters more than solo brilliance in most teams.
tips: Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Say 'I' for your actions, 'we' for the team result.
Quantify the result.
behavioral.model: Situation: our monthly sales report was late every month because three teams fed it by hand. Task: I was asked to help automate it with an engineer and a finance analyst. Action: I mapped every manual step, wrote the SQL transformations, and set up a weekly check-in so finance could validate numbers early. Result: the report was delivered on day 2 instead of day 8, and finance stopped finding errors after release.

behavioral.q: Describe a disagreement with a colleague or manager. How did you handle it?
behavioral.why: They look for maturity: facts, listening, and a solution, not a winner.
tips: Choose a professional disagreement (approach, priority), not a personal one.
Show you listened and used data.
End with the outcome and what the relationship became.
behavioral.model: My manager wanted to add a new KPI to the dashboard immediately; I thought the data was not reliable yet. I asked for 30 minutes, showed three examples where the source was wrong, and proposed a version with a data quality warning while we fixed the source. He agreed, we shipped the KPI two weeks later without errors, and he later asked me to review data sources before any new KPI.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a mistake you made and what you learned.
behavioral.why: Everyone fails; they check honesty and whether you learn.
tips: Pick a real but recoverable mistake.
Spend most of the time on the fix and the lesson.
Show the change you made so it does not happen again.
behavioral.model: I once deployed a SQL change that doubled some revenue figures because a join duplicated rows. I spotted it the next morning, warned the users before they shared the numbers, fixed the join and re-ran the report. Since then I always compare row counts and totals before and after a change, and I added an automated uniqueness test on that key.

behavioral.q: How do you handle several urgent requests at the same time?
behavioral.why: Prioritisation is a daily reality in data, BA and support roles.
tips: Explain your method: impact, urgency, deadlines, who decides.
Show you communicate trade-offs.
Give a concrete example.
behavioral.model: I list the requests with their impact and deadline, then agree the order with the requesters or my manager when they conflict. During a quarter close I had three urgent requests; I delivered the finance one first because it blocked the close, gave the other two a realistic time, and sent a short status at the end of each day. Everyone got what they needed on time.

behavioral.q: Tell me about something you improved without being asked.
behavioral.why: They want people who see problems and act.
tips: Show how you spotted the problem.
Explain how you convinced others if needed.
Give the measurable impact.
behavioral.model: I noticed analysts spent hours answering the same questions about our KPIs. I wrote a one-page glossary with definitions and example queries, and linked it from the dashboard. Questions to the team dropped by about half within a month, and the glossary is now part of onboarding.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a time you had to learn something new quickly.
behavioral.why: Tools change fast; they test how you learn.
tips: Name the skill, the deadline and your method.
Mention resources and who you asked.
Show the result and that you kept learning.
behavioral.model: My team adopted Airflow two weeks before a migration deadline. I followed the official tutorial, rebuilt one of our cron jobs as a DAG, and asked a senior engineer to review it. I then wrote a short guide for the team. We migrated all 12 jobs on time.

behavioral.q: Explain a technical topic to a non-technical person: how do you do it?
behavioral.why: Every data, BA and support role talks to business people.
tips: Start from their goal, not the technology.
Use an analogy and one example.
Check understanding and avoid jargon.
behavioral.model: When I explained why a dashboard was 'one day behind', I compared the data pipeline to a newspaper: the articles are written during the day and printed overnight, so this morning's paper shows yesterday. Then I showed which numbers were real-time and which were daily. The sales team stopped reporting it as a bug.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a difficult stakeholder or client.
behavioral.why: They check patience, empathy and firmness.
tips: Describe behaviour, not personality.
Show you understood their pressure.
End with a better working relationship.
behavioral.model: A regional director rejected every report we sent. I asked to watch how he used them and understood he needed figures by store, not by region, for his Monday meeting. We built a one-page view for that meeting; he became one of our main supporters and asked for the same view for his managers.

behavioral.q: Tell me about a time you influenced a decision without authority.
behavioral.why: Most impact comes from convincing, not commanding.
tips: Explain the decision and why it mattered.
Show your arguments: data, prototypes, allies.
Give the outcome.
behavioral.model: I wanted the team to add tests to our SQL models, but there was no time planned. I added tests to one critical model on my own, showed in the retrospective that they caught two bugs in a week, and proposed adding one test per model we touched. The team adopted it, and incidents on reports dropped noticeably.

behavioral.q: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
tips: Strength: tied to the job, with an example.
Weakness: real, not a disguised strength, with what you do about it.
behavioral.model: My strength is making messy data reliable: in my last job I cleaned our customer table and cut duplicate accounts by 30%. A weakness is that I used to say yes to every request; I now write down requests and agree priorities with my manager each week, which made my deadlines much more reliable.

behavioral.q: Where do you see yourself in 3 to 5 years?
behavioral.why: They check your ambition fits what they can offer.
tips: Show growth within the role's field.
Mention skills you want to build there.
Avoid 'in your job' or 'starting my own company'.
behavioral.model: I'd like to be a senior data engineer who owns a part of the platform end to end, mentors juniors, and works closely with analysts to make data easy to use. This role is a great step because it combines building pipelines with direct contact with the people who use the data.

behavioral.why: They check you are in budget; your answer anchors the negotiation.
tips: Research the market (job offers, Glassdoor, APEC, the Marché du travail data).
Give a range whose bottom is acceptable for you.
Say it is gross annual and that the whole package matters.
behavioral.model: Based on similar roles in Paris and my experience, I'm looking at 48 to 54k euros gross per year. I'm also interested in the whole package, such as remote days and training budget, so I'm open to discussing it.

ask: What would success look like in this role after 3 and 12 months?
What are the biggest challenges the team is facing right now?
How does the team work day to day: rituals, tools, who do I work with most?
How do you measure the quality of the team's work?
What does onboarding look like for the first weeks?
What learning or training opportunities are there?
What are the next steps in the process, and when can I expect an answer?

before: Re-read the job offer and list the 5 skills they insist on.
Check your CV fit on HelloKhedma and prepare an honest answer for each missing skill.
Research the company: product, customers, recent news, tech blog, Glassdoor reviews.
Look up your interviewers on LinkedIn.
Prepare 5 STAR stories that cover teamwork, conflict, failure, pressure and impact.
Video call: test camera, microphone, link and a quiet place. On site: plan the route, arrive 10 minutes early.
during: Listen to the whole question; it's fine to take a few seconds to think.
Answer with STAR and numbers, in 1–2 minutes per answer.
For technical questions, think aloud and state assumptions.
If you don't know, say how you would find out.
Take short notes of names and key points.
Ask your questions and the next steps.
after: Send a short thank-you email within 24 hours, mentioning one point from the conversation.
Write down the questions you were asked and how you could answer better.
Update the application in HelloKhedma: stage, notes, follow-up date.
No answer by the promised date: follow up politely once.

salary: Let them make the first number when possible; if asked, give a researched range.
Negotiate after the offer, not during the first interview.
Discuss the full package: fixed, variable, remote days, training, equipment, start date.
Ask for time to think; 24–48 hours is normal.
Be specific and polite: 'Based on the market and my experience, could we get to 52k?'

Know your rights: an EU directive (2023/970) will require employers to give the pay range in the job ad or before the first interview, and will ban questions about your current or past salary. France plans to apply it in 2027; until then you can already decline politely and give the range you expect instead.
